Separation
sep-uh-RAY-shun
n.
From Latin separatio, a setting apart. Webster 1828: the act of separating; disjunction; the state of being separate. In the Authorized Version the noun is technical in three places — the Nazarite’s vow, the woman’s ceremonial uncleanness, and the water of separation made with the ashes of the red heifer.

Biblical Definition

Separation in the law is a defined period or a defined substance, not a mood. The Nazarite’s vow is measured in days of separation: All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk (Numbers 6:4), and the reason is stated without qualification: All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD (Numbers 6:8). When the term is complete he shall be brought unto the door of the tabernacle (Numbers 6:13). The second use is the woman’s ceremonial uncleanness, regulated in Leviticus 12 and 15 — every thing that she lieth upon in her separation shall be unclean (Leviticus 15:20). The third is a liquid: the water of separation, made from the ashes of the red heifer, which purified the man defiled by a dead body, and which paradoxically defiled the man who prepared it (Numbers 19:21). Ezekiel’s temple has the principle built into stone: a wall to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place (Ezekiel 42:20). The doctrine running through all four is that holiness has boundaries, and God draws them Himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SEPARATION as the act of separating or disjoining; the state of being separate; and, in law, a partial divorce. The KJV uses the noun in its ceremonial senses: a period of vow, a period of uncleanness, and a purifying water.

expand to see more

SEPARATION, n. — The act of separating, or state of being separate; disjunction.

The operation of disuniting or decomposing substances; analysis.

In a legal sense, the parting of husband and wife without a dissolution of the marriage bond.

The biblical noun is narrower than Webster’s English. In Numbers 6 it names the whole period of the vow, so that the days themselves are called his separation — the man is not merely doing something separate; he is a separated thing for a term.

Key Scripture

Numbers 6:4 — "All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk."

Numbers 6:8 — "All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD."

Numbers 6:13 — "And this is the law of the Nazarite, when the days of his separation are fulfilled: he shall be brought unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation:"

Numbers 19:21 — "And it shall be a perpetual statute unto them, that he that sprinkleth the water of separation shall wash his clothes; and he that toucheth the water of separation shall be unclean until even."

Ezekiel 42:20 — "He measured it by the four sides: it had a wall round about, five hundred reeds long, and five hundred broad, to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place."

Modern Corruption

Separation is corrupted in two directions: by a church that has erased every boundary between the sanctuary and the profane, and by a separatism that keeps drawing new lines until it has divided from everyone but itself.

expand to see more

Ezekiel 42:20 states the purpose of a wall: to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place. The distinction is God’s, and a church that has lost it will not be more accessible but merely indistinguishable. The New Testament does not abolish the distinction; it relocates it, since the church is now the temple of the living God, which is why Paul quotes Isaiah at the Corinthians — come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you (2 Corinthians 6:17). What that requires is not withdrawal from society, which Paul explicitly denies in 1 Corinthians 5:10, but the refusal of unequal yokes and of tolerated sin within the assembly.

The opposite error has a long and unhappy history among those who take the doctrine seriously. Secondary separation — refusing fellowship not only with the unfaithful but with the faithful who have not refused them — has fractured churches into ever smaller remnants, each certain it has kept the wall. Numbers 6 is a useful corrective: the Nazarite’s separation was for a term, was defined by God down to the grape husk, and ended at the door of the tabernacle with a sacrifice and a return to the congregation. It was a vow within the covenant people, not an exit from them, and it had a boundary drawn by God rather than extended by the man.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew nouns differ by context: nezer is the Nazarite’s consecration, niddah the ceremonial uncleanness, and me niddah the water of separation. The unifying root idea is being set apart or put away.

expand to see more

Hebrew nezer (H5145) — consecration, separation, a crown; the Nazarite’s vow and the diadem on the high priest’s mitre (Numbers 6:4, 8, 13).

Hebrew nazir (H5139) — one separated, a Nazarite; the noun for the man under the vow.

Hebrew niddah (H5079) — separation, impurity; the ceremonial state of Leviticus 12:5 and 15:20.

Hebrew me niddah — water of separation, the ash-water of the red heifer (Numbers 19:21), which cleansed the defiled and defiled the clean.

Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, separate; the verb of Genesis 1 and of Ezekiel’s wall between sanctuary and profane.

Usage

"All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD (Numbers 6:8) — the vow makes the whole period, and the man, a set-apart thing."

"The water of separation (Numbers 19:21) — a purifying water that defiled the man who handled it; a type of the cleansing that costs the cleanser."

"To make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place (Ezekiel 42:20) — the distinction built into the architecture."
